name: ATSAMD09D14A-MUT
title: SAM D09 Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 48 MHz, 8 or 16 KB Flash, 4 KB SRAM, 14 and 24 pins
summary: A small low-power 32-bit microcontroller series built on the Arm Cortex-M0+ core at up to 48 MHz, running from one 2.4 V to 3.63 V supply. It has 8 or 16 KB of in-system programmable Flash, 4 KB of SRAM, a six-channel DMA controller, a six-channel event system, two 16-bit timer/counters, a 32-bit RTC with calendar, two SERCOM serial blocks (USART, SPI, I2C, SMBus/PMBus, LIN slave) and a 12-bit 350 ksps ADC with up to 10 channels, gain and oversampling to 16 bits. ATSAMD09D14A-MUT is the 16 KB part in a 24-pin QFN with 22 I/O pins, on tape and reel; the ATSAMD09C13A-SSUT is the 8 KB part in a 14-pin SOIC.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ (r0p1), up to 48 MHz, single-cycle multiplier, Micro Trace Buffer
16 KB Flash (ATSAMD09D14A) or 8 KB (ATSAMD09C13A), 4 KB SRAM

operation.text: SAM D09 parts share peripherals, a linear address map and hex-compatible code with the rest of the SAM D family, so firmware moves up to larger devices; pins also migrate within the series. The core reaches 2.46 CoreMark/MHz. Capacitive touch buttons, sliders and wheels are supported.

Two sleep modes, chosen in software. Idle stops the CPU and can keep everything else running. Standby stops every clock and function except those set to keep running. With SleepWalking a peripheral wakes on its own condition (a threshold crossed, a result ready) and wakes the CPU only when that is met. The event system passes synchronous and asynchronous events between peripherals in standby too.

Flash is reprogrammed in the system over the two-pin SWD port, which also serves debugging and trace on chip without disturbing the running code. A bootloader in the part may load new application code over any of the communication interfaces.

An Arm Cortex-M0+ CPU at up to 48 MHz with a single-cycle hardware multiplier and a Micro Trace Buffer; 8 or 16 KB of self-programmable Flash and 4 KB of SRAM; up to 22 I/O pins; operation from 2.4 V to 3.63 V; 24-pin QFN and 14-pin SOIC packages. The ADC is 12-bit at 350 ksps with up to 10 channels.

Six DMA channels and six event-system channels; eight external interrupts plus one NMI; two 16-bit timer/counters, each usable as 8 or 16 bit, or paired as one 32-bit counter, with compare/capture channels and waveform outputs; a 32-bit RTC with calendar; a watchdog; a CRC-32 generator. Each of the two SERCOMs can be a full-duplex or single-wire half-duplex USART, I2C, SMBus/PMBus, SPI or LIN slave. The ADC takes single-ended or differential inputs through a 1/2x to 16x gain stage, corrects offset and gain error itself, and oversamples and decimates in hardware to 13, 14, 15 or 16 bits.

Every oscillator can drive the system clock: crystal oscillators for 0.4 to 32 MHz and 32.768 kHz, internal 8 MHz, 32.768 kHz and ultra-low-power 32 kHz oscillators, the 48 MHz DFLL and a fractional PLL from 48 to 96 MHz. Clock domains are set independently, so each peripheral can run at its own frequency.
Software identifies the device from DSU.DID.DEVSEL. The low 16 bits of the DID reset value hold the die number, the die revision and the device selection.
Every pin is a PORT general-purpose I/O by default. Setting PINCFGn.PMUXEN (n = 0 to 31) gives the pin to a peripheral, and PMUXn.PMUXE/O picks which of functions A, B, C, D, E, G or H.

The crystal oscillators are not PORT functions; SYSCTRL registers connect them to PA08 and PA09. Of the debug pins only SWCLK is a PORT function. When a debugger is plugged in, cold or hot, PA31 is switched to SWDIO without software.

VDDIO/IN/ANA supplies the I/O lines, OSC8M, XOSC, the internal regulator, the ADC, OSCULP32K, OSC32K and XOSC32K, from 2.4 V to 3.63 V. The regulator makes the 1.2 V that runs the core, memories, peripherals, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M. PA02 to PA07 sit beside the ADC; PA08 and PA09 beside XOSC. GND is the ground pin.
Normal mode serves the CPU and peripherals running. Low-power mode draws little static current and suits standby.
For the POR to work, VDDIO/IN/ANA must ramp up no slower than a minimum rate and no faster than a maximum rate; the electrical characteristics give both.

The device holds itself in reset after power-up until the supply has settled everywhere. It then starts on 1 MHz: OSC8M divided by eight, fed to generic clock generator 0, which clocks the Power Manager. Some synchronous system clocks run, undivided, at that 1 MHz so code can execute. Of the generic clocks only GCLK_WDT, for the watchdog, is on.
After power-up every I/O pin is left high-impedance.
When reset is released the CPU loads its PC and SP from address 0x00000000, the start of internal Flash. That code then sets up the clock system.

Three monitors. POR watches VDDIO/IN/ANA at all times, including every sleep mode, and resets the whole chip when it falls below threshold. BOD33 watches the 3.3 V supply and is set up in SYSCTRL. BOD12 watches the internal VDDCORE after start-up; it is calibrated in production, its settings sit in the NVM User Row and they must stay unchanged when the user row is rewritten.

High-speed Flash, high-speed SRAM with single-cycle access at full speed, and a Flash area set aside for EEPROM emulation. The high-speed bus is a bus matrix with fixed addresses; nothing is remapped, not even at boot.
Read at 0x804000 and loaded automatically at power-on; NVMCTRL writes it. A new value takes effect in the other modules only after the next reset.
Read at 0x806020 and not writable. It holds production-measured calibration values that application code copies into the matching registers itself.

Arm Cortex-M0+ revision r0p1, ARMv6 architecture with the Thumb-2 instruction set; it is instruction-set compatible with the Cortex-M0 and upward compatible with the M3 and M4. Two buses: a 32-bit AHB-Lite system interface to Flash, RAM and peripherals, and a 32-bit single-cycle I/O port straight to the PORT registers. The two work concurrently, so instruction fetches continue during I/O and single-cycle I/O can be kept up indefinitely.
The System Control Space holds the debug registers. SysTick is a 24-bit timer. The System Control Block reports and controls configuration and system exceptions.
The NVIC takes 32 external interrupts at 4 priority levels, set per interrupt in software. It is tightly coupled to the core for low latency and quick handling of late-arriving interrupts.
A symmetric crossbar switch with a 32-bit data bus, running at the same clock as the masters, letting different masters reach different slaves at the same time.

Each master reaching the SRAM carries its own QoS level. At level 0x00 or 0x01 a RAM access costs at least one cycle of latency. Concurrent accesses are ordered first by QoS level, then by SRAM port ID, the lowest ID first. The MTB is fixed at level 3 and the DSU at level 1. The CPU level is bits [1:0] at 0x41007110, reset 0x0; the DMAC level is set in its own QOSCTRL register.

An AHB slave giving access to the peripherals' control registers in the low-power APB domain. It follows AMBA APB Protocol Specification V2.0 (APB4): wait states, error reporting, transaction protection and sparse byte, half-word and word transfers. It adds address and data cycles merged into one cycle and sparse transfers on reads too. CLK_HPBx_AHB must be on for the bridge to work.

One PAC per bridge write-protects the registers of each peripheral on that bridge. At reset the PAC0 and PAC1 bus clocks (CLK_PAC0_APB, CLK_PAC1_APB) run and CLK_PAC2_APB does not; the PAC keeps working in any sleep mode whose clock runs. A debugger ignores the protection. Writing one to a bit of WPCLR lifts protection for that peripheral, writing one to WPSET applies it; both registers read back the same value. A write to a protected peripheral is dropped with an access error (CPU exception). Protecting an already protected peripheral, or unprotecting an unprotected one, also raises an error (CPU exception), which can be used to check program flow; WPSET reads back the current protection status.

The Device Service Unit detects debug probes, lets the Arm Debug Access Port take the debug pads and CPU reset, holds a CoreSight ROM for device identification, and offers memory services (CRC32, MBIST) such as IEC60730 Class B testing needs. It sits on the bus matrix, so debugger and CPU can use it together. Its features: CPU reset extension, cold- and hot-plug probe detection, chip erase, CRC32 over any memory on the bus matrix, two debug communication channels, a DAP security filter and memory built-in self-test. Some are limited while the NVMCTRL security bit is set.

SWCLK belongs to the DSU by default for probe detection and reset extension. Changing its PORT function or disabling its PORT mux turns hot-plugging off until a power or external reset. The DSU runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs; the PM gates its APB and AHB clocks (CLK_DSU_APB, CLK_DSU_AHB). It has no interrupts, events or analog connections. All writable registers except DCC0 and DCC1 can be write-protected by the PAC; a debugger ignores that protection.

If SWCLK is low when RESET is released, the CPU stays in reset so a debugger can connect before code runs, and STATUSA.CRSTEXT reads one. Writing one to STATUSA.CRSTEXT releases the CPU and clears the bit; writing zero does nothing. SWCLK has an internal pull-up at start-up so a floating pin does not look like a debugger. While the security bit is set the CPU cannot be released this way, and trying sets STATUSA.PERR.

Cold-plugging finds a debugger while the system is in reset, through the reset extension. Hot-plugging finds one while the system runs, on a falling edge of SWCLK; it cannot work during reset, as POR and RESET reset the detector, and it needs SWCLK left on its debug function (STATUSB.HPE shows whether it is available). Either detection sets STATUSB.DBGPRES. Hot-plugging is unavailable while the security bit is set. Detection needs powered pads, so at cold start it waits for the POR release; on a protected device only cold-plugging can find a probe, so the external reset must outlast the POR, and if reset is released before POR the attempt is repeated until it connects.

Chip erase clears all volatile memory and the Flash array, EEPROM emulation area included, and removes the security bit; the auxiliary rows, user row included, are kept. It starts on a write of one to CTRL.CE, is ignored while the PAC protects the DSU, and is done when STATUSA.DONE reads one. A protected device must be reset by the debugger to be detected. The sequence: cold-plug so the probe is found and the CPU held in reset; write CTRL.CE (volatile memory cleared, Flash array erased, lock row erased); poll STATUSA.DONE; reset so NVMCTRL reloads the fuses.

Programming needs the security bit clear. The debugger holds RESET low at power-up; the regulator keeps the system in POR until the supply passes the POR threshold and the internal supplies settle. The PM starts and switches clocks to the slow clock while the external reset holds the internal resets. With SWCLK held low, releasing RESET cold-plugs the debugger; the debugger then clocks SWCLK and the DAP runs. The CPU stays in reset while the rest of the system starts; a chip erase clears Flash, and programming goes through the AHB-AP. Afterwards the chip restarts on RESET, a power cycle or a write of one to STATUSA.CRSTEXT; SWCLK must be high at RESET release so the CPU is not held again.

Setting the NVMCTRL security bit shuts external tools out of the internal memories until a chip erase. The DSU filters the AHB-AP's transactions: on a protected device an access outside the DSU external range is dropped and answered with an error, raising the AHB-AP sticky error bits. The CPU uses the DSU without limit even when protected. The first 0x100 bytes of DSU registers are the internal range and are mirrored at offset 0x100 as the external range; a protected device lets the DAP make MEM-AP accesses only between offsets 0x100 and 0x2000, and accesses at 0x100 to 0x1FF are then restricted.

A CoreSight ROM table, whose address is in the DAP's MEM-AP BASE register, identifies the vendor and the way to identify the chip, through a 64-bit ID built from PID0 to PID7. The DID register then gives the processor, family, subfamily and device select.

CRC32 and MBIST share ADDR, LENGTH and DATA: set them, then issue the command in CTRL. Any other command is ignored until STATUSA.DONE is set. Enabling the clocks enables the module; its registers can be write-protected by the PAC. A debug adapter uses the external range 0x100 to 0x2000, and on a protected device an access to the first 0x100 bytes returns an error; the CPU uses the internal range 0x0 to 0x100.

The DSU computes a CRC32 over a memory area, Flash or AHB RAM. It uses the standard CRC32 polynomial 0xEDB88320 in reversed form. ADDR takes the word-aligned start and LENGTH the word-aligned size; DATA takes the starting value, normally 0xFFFFFFFF, or an earlier result to chain several blocks. CTRL.CRC starts it and CTRL.SWRST cancels it. When STATUSA.DONE sets, check STATUSA.BERR for a bus error, then read DATA; complement it to match the usual CRC32, or keep it as it is to seed the next run. From the internal range any area can be checked; from the external range on a protected device only the whole Flash array or whole EEPROM area, with the registers forced, which lets a protected part be verified.

DCC0 and DCC1 are two registers with handshake that CPU and debugger can both use, even on a protected device, at run time and in debug mode, for a custom debug protocol. STATUSB.DCC0D and DCC1D set on write and clear on read. On a protected device a debugger cannot attach while the CPU runs. MBIST uses the same registers, so they must stay idle during MBIST.

MBIST runs a March LR test, linear in time, that finds address decoder, stuck-at, transition, coupling, linked coupling and stuck-open faults; its run time depends on the CPU clock and the number of RAM bytes. It is meant mainly for production test and cannot run from the external range on a protected device (STATUSA.PERR is set). ADDR.ADDR takes the start and LENGTH the size; testing a whole physical memory gives the best coverage. CTRL.MBIST starts it and CTRL.SWRST cancels it. With ADDR.AMOD = 0 (the default) it stops at the first fault or at the end, sets STATUSA.DONE, and sets STATUSA.FAIL on a fault. With ADDR.AMOD = 1 it pauses on a fault with only STATUSA.FAIL set and resumes when one is written to STATUSA.FAIL. On a fault ADDR holds the word address and DATA the failing bit and phase.
An external access is one at DSU offsets 0x200 to 0x1FFF; an internal access is one at offsets 0x0 to 0x100.

Clocks come in three layers. SYSCTRL runs the clock sources (XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M, FDPLL96M). GCLK has generic clock generators, each a prescaler that can take any source, and generic clock multiplexers that hand one generator's output to a peripheral as its generic clock; separate instances of a peripheral usually have separate generic clocks. Generator 0 is GCLK_MAIN, which feeds the PM. Generic clock 0 is the DFLL48M reference when the DFLL multiplies another clock. The PM makes the synchronous clocks: CPU, AHB and APB bus clocks and the bus interfaces of the peripherals, with a mask bit per interface and prescalers for the CPU and bus clocks. For example, SERCOM0 run from DFLL48M in open loop uses generator 1 sourced from DFLL48M, generic clock 20 (GCLK_SERCOM0_CORE) set to generator 1, and CLK_SERCOM0_APB unmasked in the PM APBC mask.

Synchronous clocks are the CPU and bus clocks; asynchronous clocks are the generic clocks. Where a CPU access crosses into a peripheral's generic clock domain the peripheral synchronizes it and shows a SYNCBUSY flag. GCLK, WDT, RTC, EIC, TC and ADC use one common synchronizer per peripheral; SERCOM USART, SPI and I2C (and I2S) use a distributed synchronizer, one per register.

The bus interface registers need no synchronization. Every core register in the generic clock domain is synchronized on write, and some on read; only one register per peripheral can be in synchronization at a time. A write to a core register sets STATUS.SYNCBUSY until it completes. While it is set, writing a core register, reading a read-synchronized register, or reading the register being written stalls the bus; other core registers and APB registers read without a stall. Reading a read-synchronized register always stalls the bus until done, without setting SYNCBUSY, and stalls twice if a synchronization was already running. Completion is seen by polling SYNCBUSY, by the synchronization-ready interrupt where present, or by simply issuing the next access.

Peripherals with a READREQ register avoid read stalls: writing READREQ.RREQ with the register offset in READREQ.ADDR starts one read synchronization (SYNCBUSY set while it runs) and the value then reads without delay until RREQ is written again. READREQ.RCONT keeps synchronizing the register continuously so the latest value is always available; SYNCBUSY is set only for the first one. A write to a write-synchronized register stops a continuous request, which must then be restarted, and continuous synchronization pauses in sleep modes where the generic clock stops.

Writing CTRL.ENABLE or one to CTRL.SWRST also starts a write synchronization and sets SYNCBUSY (in the distributed scheme SYNCBUSY.ENABLE or SYNCBUSY.SWRST). ENABLE reads its new value at once; SWRST reads one at once and it and SYNCBUSY clear when the reset is done; writing zero to SWRST does nothing. During either, a write to any core or APB register or a read of a read-synchronized register stalls the bus; APB registers still read without a stall. The synchronization-ready interrupt cannot signal these two.

Each write-synchronized core register has its own synchronizer and its own SYNCBUSY bit, so different registers can be written back to back. A second write to the same register before its synchronization ends is discarded: writing a 16-bit register as two 8-bit writes loses the second and flags an error, while one 16-bit write is fine. A 32-bit write covering several registers writes them all, though each may update at a different time. A core register reads immediately, but the value is only reliable when its SYNCBUSY bit is clear.

A peripheral on a generic clock needs a running clock source, an enabled generic clock generator using it, its generic clock enabled and pointed at that generator, and its bus interface unmasked in the PM. Without the mask bit its registers read as zero and writes are lost.

Every clock source can run on demand: stopped while no peripheral requests it, started when a request arrives through the generic clock and generator, which must both be enabled. Clearing a source's ONDEMAND bit keeps it always running, removing its start-up time at the cost of power. In standby the request mechanism still works for modules set to run in standby (RUNSTDBY).
A slow generic clock lowers a peripheral's active power but lengthens synchronization with the CPU domain, so responses are slower and more time is spent waiting.

On any reset OSC8M is enabled with division by 8, GCLK_MAIN runs from OSC8M, and the CPU and bus clocks are undivided. On a power reset every generic clock generator is disabled except generator 0 (GCLK_MAIN, OSC8M, no division) and generator 2 (OSCULP32K, no division), and every generic clock is disabled except the WDT's, which uses generator 2. A user reset does the same except for write-locked generic clocks (WRTLOCK set before the reset, or the WDT clock when the WDT Always-On bit is set in the NVM User Row) and the RTC's generic clock if it is enabled. Clock sources return to their reset state on any reset, except the 32 kHz sources, which only a power reset resets.

The Generic Clock Controller has eight generic clock generators feeding m generic clock multiplexers, m set by the number of peripherals. Each generator takes an internal or external source, optionally divides it, and its output can serve one or more multiplexers; each multiplexer picks one generator to make one peripheral's generic clock (GCLK_PERIPHERAL), which may serve one or several peripherals. A generator's source can be changed while running. GCLK works in all sleep modes and has no interrupts, events or debug behaviour; its registers can be write-protected by the PAC. Its bus clock CLK_GCLK_APB is gated in the PM (APBAMASK).

Enable the generator's clock source first. Then: one 32-bit write to GENDIV with the generator number in GENDIV.ID and the division factor in GENDIV.DIV; one 32-bit write to GENCTRL with the generator in GENCTRL.ID and GENEN set; one 16-bit write to CLKCTRL with the generic clock in CLKCTRL.ID and the generator in CLKCTRL.GEN. The module has no enable bit. CTRL.SWRST resets every register except generic clocks and their generators that are write-locked.

Each generator can use one of eight sources; generator 1 has seven, since it can be a source to the others but not to itself. Generator x pairs with pin GCLK_IO[x], which can be its input or show its output. The source can be divided and each generator enabled on its own (GENCTRL.GENEN); when GENEN reads zero the output is gated off. Generator 0 is GCLK_MAIN for the PM. Changing GENCTRL.SRC from source A to B happens on the fly: the generator keeps running on A until B is ready, holding requests to both, then releases A. GENCTRL.DIVSEL chooses how GENDIV.DIV is read; the number of DIV bits differs per generator. An odd division gives an uneven duty cycle unless GENCTRL.IDC is set, which gives 50/50.

operation.topic: Generic clock output on a pin
operation.text: With GENCTRL.OE and GENEN set the generator requests its source and drives GCLK_IO. With OE clear the pin sits at GENCTRL.OOV (low if 0, high if 1) while the generator is off. In standby an output pin freezes at OOV unless GENCTRL.RUNSTDBY is set, which keeps the clock running out to the pin.

Select a generator in CLKCTRL.GEN, then set CLKCTRL.CLKEN; CLKEN is synchronized into the generic clock domain and reads its old value until done. Clearing CLKEN gates the clock off. To change a running clock's generator without glitches: write CLKEN to zero, wait until it reads zero, write CLKCTRL.GEN, set CLKEN again. Setting CLKCTRL.WRTLOCK locks the clock's CLKCTRL and its generator's GENCTRL and GENDIV until a power reset; SWRST does not unlock them. Generator 0 cannot be locked and returns to a known setting on every reset.

GENCTRL, GENDIV and CLKCTRL are reached through an ID field: a write carries the generator or clock number in ID. To read one, first do an 8-bit write of the number to the ID field, then read the register. The reset settings of generators and clocks depend on the device.

When generic clocks are off in sleep, any peripheral needing its own clock asks for it; GCLK wakes the source and turns on the generator and clock in turn (SleepWalking). In standby GCLK can keep driving a generator output to GCLK_IO. GENCTRL, GENDIV and CTRL are write-synchronized: STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done, and another synchronized operation while it is set stalls the bus, holding the CPU and leaving interrupts pending.

The Power Manager controls reset, synchronous clock generation and sleep modes. It divides CLK_MAIN (from GCLK_MAIN) into a CPU-and-AHB clock domain plus a domain per APB bridge, each changeable at run time and maskable per module. A clock failure detector can move the main clock to OSC8M if it stops. Its reset controller gathers the reset sources: power resets POR, BOD12 and BOD33; user resets from the RESET pin, the watchdog and software; RCAUSE tells software which happened. The CPU/AHB/APB prescaler divides by 1 to 128. Sleep modes are IDLE and STANDBY, with SleepWalking on GCLK clocks. In standby the regulator runs in low-power mode, so enough clocks and peripherals must be off first not to overload it.

CLK_PM_APB is on by default; if turned off only a reset brings it back. CLK_MAIN feeds a common 8-bit prescaler for the CPU, AHB and APB clocks. Stopping CLK_CPU stops instruction execution. CLK_AHB is synchronous to and the same frequency as the CPU clock but can run with the CPU clock off; CLK_APBx is synchronous to the CPU clock, can be divided, and also runs with the CPU clock off. Each module's AHB or APB clock has its own gate. In debug the PM keeps clocks running in sleep so the debugger can reach modules, so power cannot be measured in debug mode. INTFLAG and RCAUSE are never write-protected by the PAC.

After a power-on reset RCAUSE shows POR, the GCLK_MAIN source is started and calibrated before the CPU runs, and the main clock is used undivided; only the needed peripheral clocks are on. The PM is always enabled and cannot be reset. CPUSEL.CPUDIV sets the CPU clock and APBxSEL.APBxDIV each APB clock, always with fCPU ≥ fAPBx and every domain within its maximum frequency; the AHB clock always equals the CPU clock. CPUSEL and APBxSEL can be written while peripherals run, so the CPU can be scaled while the APB frequency stays the same. After a write, INTFLAG.CKRDY reads zero until the new setting takes effect (it can raise the PM interrupt). Rewriting CPUSEL before CKRDY returns to one can hang the system.

Each AHB or APB peripheral clock is turned on or off by its bit in the APBxMASK or AHBMASK registers; a module on several domains has several bits. A module with its APB clock off cannot be read or written. Turning off NVMCTRL's clock breaks Flash reads by the CPU; turning off the PM's clock or its APB bridge leaves the mask registers unwritable until a system reset.

With CTRL.CFDEN set the detector watches the undivided main clock and calls it failed if no rising edge comes within one OSCULP32K period. It then switches the main clock to OSC8M, sets INTFLAG.CFD (interrupt if enabled) and sets CTRL.BKUPCLK; writing BKUPCLK to zero selects GCLK_MAIN again but does not cure the failure. It is blind while the main clock is briefly absent (start-up after wake-up) or in sleep, and must be disabled before standby. It must not be used unless the main clock is much faster than OSCULP32K (not with the 32 kHz RC as main clock), and OSC8M should be enabled so the switch can happen.

RCAUSE holds the latest reset cause for the boot code. Power resets come from electrical events (POR, BOD12, BOD33, all from SYSCTRL); user resets from the application: the RESET pin pulled low, the watchdog, and SysResetReq, the CPU's SYSRESETREQ bit in its reset control register. RESET has an internal pull-up and needs no drive in normal operation.

WFI enters sleep; SLEEP.IDLE and the CPU's SCR.SLEEPDEEP choose the mode. IDLE stops the CPU and, by level, more synchronous clock domains, with the regulator in normal mode; the modules are halted whatever their mask bits. IDLE is entered by WFI with SLEEPDEEP = 0 after setting SLEEP.IDLE, or on leaving the lowest-priority ISR when SCR.SLEEPONEXIT is set, and is left on any interrupt unmasked in the NVIC with enough priority. STANDBY (WFI with SLEEPDEEP = 1, SLEEPONEXIT also available) stops every clock except those a running module requests or whose ONDEMAND is zero (with RUNSTDBY), e.g. the RTC and its generic clock source; regulator and RAM go to low-power mode. Any peripheral that can raise an asynchronous interrupt wakes it, and the device then runs the ISR or continues according to PRIMASK. In IDLE the PM runs on the main clock; in STANDBY it is frozen until an asynchronous interrupt.

SleepWalking lets a peripheral wake its clocks briefly in STANDBY to do a task without waking the CPU; afterwards it either wakes the device with an interrupt or the device stays in STANDBY. On this device it works only for GCLK clocks, through on-demand clock requests. The PM interrupts are clock ready (CKRDY) and clock failure (CFD); each has a flag in INTFLAG, set in INTENSET, cleared in INTENCLR, and the flag is cleared by writing one to it. The PM has no events.

The System Controller is the register interface to the clock sources, the brown-out detectors, the core voltage regulator and the voltage reference. Each block is enabled, disabled, calibrated and watched through it; their status bits are gathered in PCLKSR and can raise interrupts through INTENSET, INTENCLR and INTFLAG, and BOD33 and BOD12 interrupts can wake the device from standby. Blocks: XOSC, a 0.4-32 MHz crystal oscillator with adjustable gain and start-up time, or an external clock on XIN; XOSC32K, a 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator with automatic or manual gain and adjustable start-up, or an external clock on XIN32; OSC32K, a 32.768 kHz high-accuracy internal oscillator with fine tuning and adjustable start-up; OSCULP32K, a 32.768 kHz ultra-low-power always-on oscillator with fine tuning, calibrated from Flash at reset; OSC8M, an 8 MHz internal oscillator with fast start-up, fine tuning and 4, 2 and 1 MHz divided outputs, calibrated from Flash at reset; DFLL48M, a 48 MHz loop needing no external parts, an open-loop oscillator or a closed-loop multiplier of a known clock; FDPLL96M, a fractional digital PLL giving 48 to 96 MHz from a 32 kHz to 2 MHz reference, with three reference choices, an adjustable PI controller and 1/16 steps of the reference; BOD33 and BOD12, brown-out detectors with programmable threshold loaded from Flash at start-up, reset or interrupt action, continuous or sampled mode and hysteresis; VREF, a bandgap with calibration loaded from Flash and a temperature sensor; and VREG, the core regulator, with its trim loaded from Flash.

SYSCTRL supplies XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M to GCLK. CLK_SYSCTRL_APB is gated in the PM. The BOD sampling clock and the DFLL48M control logic run asynchronously to the bus clock, so some writes need synchronization. A 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XIN32 and XOUT32 and a 0.4-32 MHz crystal between XIN and XOUT, with load capacitors as needed. In debug SYSCTRL keeps running. When debugger cold-plugging is detected the BOD33 reset is masked; under hot-plugging the BOD reset stays active. INTFLAG is never write-protected by the PAC.

The chosen reference must be set up and running before the FDPLL96M is used, and a GCLK reference must sit inside the FDPLL96M input range. XOSC can be divided inside the FDPLL96M; the divider and crystal frequency together must give a reference inside the input range. Using the internal lock timer needs a 32 kHz clock from GCLK (GCLK_DPLL_32K).

An oscillator runs only once its ENABLE bit is set. By default it runs in idle only when a peripheral requests it (ONDEMAND resets to one) and stops in standby. ONDEMAND = 0 keeps it always running in idle. RUNSTDBY = 1 lets it run in standby (not DFLL48M or FDPLL96M), on request if ONDEMAND is one and always if ONDEMAND is zero. OSCULP32K always runs and cannot be disabled.

XOSC takes either an external clock on XIN or a 0.4-32 MHz crystal. It is off at reset, leaving XIN and XOUT free as GPIO. XOSC.ENABLE turns it on; XOSC.XTALEN = 1 selects crystal mode (both pins taken over), 0 selects an external clock (only XIN taken; XOUT stays GPIO). In crystal mode XOSC.GAIN must match the crystal frequency; XOSC.AMPGC turns on automatic amplitude control, which usually lowers current. After reset or a wake-up where it was off, the output is masked for the start-up time set in XOSC.STARTUP, after which PCLKSR.XOSCRDY sets (interrupt on its rising edge if enabled). Standby must not be entered while any oscillator is starting: wait for its ready bit in PCLKSR.

XOSC32K takes an external clock on XIN32 or a 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 and XOUT32. It is off at POR with the pins free as GPIO; crystal mode (XOSC32K.XTALEN = 1) takes both pins, external clock mode only XIN32. To disable it write ENABLE to zero leaving the other bits unchanged; writing ENABLE together with other bits can give unpredictable results. Once enabled it stays on in all sleep modes. The output is masked for the start-up time in XOSC32K.STARTUP, then PCLKSR.XOSC32KRDY sets. Because a crystal can take up to one second to start, it keeps running through every reset except POR. With a crystal it gives a 32.768 kHz output (EN32K) and a 1.024 kHz output (EN1K); neither works with an external clock on XIN32.

OSC32K is a tunable low-speed low-power internal oscillator, off by default, turned on by OSC32K.ENABLE, with a 32.768 kHz output (EN32K) and a 1.024 kHz output (EN1K). Its frequency is set by OSC32K.CALIB, which software must write; the factory value is in the NVM Software Calibration Area. After writing CALIB, the value takes effect once PCLKSR.OSC32KRDY goes high.

OSCULP32K is a tunable ultra-low-power 32 kHz oscillator, factory calibrated at typical voltage and temperature; it is the choice over OSC32K when power matters more than frequency accuracy. It is on after POR and always runs except during POR, with 32.768 kHz and 1.024 kHz outputs always on. OSCULP32K.CALIB is loaded from factory calibration at start-up to correct for process and can be overwritten.

OSC8M is an open-loop 8 MHz internal oscillator, factory calibrated at typical voltage and temperature, the default clock after POR and the backup clock when the clock failure detector trips. OSC8M.ENABLE turns it on and off. OSC8M.CALIB is loaded from factory calibration at start-up; FRANGE and CALIB can be written to set the frequency; updating them while it is enabled is not recommended. Being open loop, its frequency depends on voltage, temperature and process. It is switched off automatically in some sleep modes.

Every reset selects open-loop mode, where DFLLVAL.COARSE and DFLLVAL.FINE set the output frequency; loading the DFLL48M COARSE CAL value from the calibration table into COARSE gives close to 48 MHz. COARSE and FINE may be changed while the DFLL runs. CLK_DFLL48M is usable once PCLKSR.DFLLRDY sets.

In closed loop the output is held at a multiple of a reference. After enabling the DFLL: enable a reference CLK_DFLL48M_REF, which is generic clock channel 0; set the largest coarse and fine steps in DFLLMUL.CSTEP and FSTEP (small steps give little overshoot but slower lock, large ones the reverse; neither above half the maximum of COARSE or FINE); set the multiplier DFLLMUL.MUL so the output stays below the DFLL maximum (a target below the minimum gives the minimum frequency); set DFLLCTRL.MODE. COARSE and FINE are then read-only and driven by the tuner, which starts from the COARSE value, so writing COARSE near its final value shortens coarse lock. Loading DFLL48M COARSE CAL into COARSE, setting DFLLCTRL.BPLCKC, then starting closed loop cuts lock time to the fine lock time. Locking is in two stages: coarse lock sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKC, fine lock sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKF, each able to interrupt. DFLLRDY means the clock is usable; its accuracy depends on which locks are set.

operation.topic: DFLL48M drift, reference loss and accuracy
operation.text: With DFLLCTRL.STABLE = 0 the tuner follows drift without losing lock, so FINE may change after every measurement. An unstable or drifting reference can overflow or underflow FINE, setting PCLKSR.DFLLOOB; so closed loop needs a steady reference: an external oscillator, never an internal one, with XOSC32K the preferred source. If the reference stops or falls below CLK_DFLL48M/(2 × MULMAX), PCLKSR.DFLLRCS sets, which can take around 2^17 CLK_DFLL48M cycles to detect; the DFLL then behaves as open loop and returns to closed loop when the reference comes back. A new frequency can take several microseconds to appear, which with a small MUL can upset locking: chill cycles (on by default, off with DFLLCTRL.CCDIS) skip measurement for a cycle and may double lock time; quick lock (on by default, off with DFLLCTRL.QLDIS) loosens the lock criteria, giving more spread but the same average. DFLLCTRL.LLAW = 0 keeps the locks and settings across disable (e.g. sleep), fine tracking catching up when the reference returns if STABLE = 0; LLAW = 1 drops all locks so the full sequence repeats. Accuracy depends on the fine step size (smaller at higher output frequency), the measurement resolution (a small output to reference ratio can lock low; a reference of 32 kHz or lower is recommended for low targets) and the reference accuracy.

The FDPLL96M is a digital PLL with a PI digital filter, a time-to-digital converter, a digitally controlled oscillator and a fractional feedback divider. Its reference CLK_FDPLL96M_REF is CLK_DPLL_REF0 (XOSC32K), CLK_DPLL_REF1 (XOSC, through a divider) or GCLK_DPLL; its output is CK_GATED, gated only by its own control. The internal lock timer needs a valid 32 kHz GCLK_DPLL_32K. Disabling it resets the output. LDRFRAC = 0 gives integer mode, otherwise fractional mode, which adds jitter. Example: 32 kHz reference to 48 MHz is a ratio of 1500, so LDR = 1499; to 48.006 MHz the ratio is 1500.1875 (1500 + 3/16), so LDR = 1499 and LDRFRAC = 3.

DPLLCTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off; the output is stable once enabled and DPLLSTATUS.LOCK is set. With DPLLCTRLB.LTIME non-zero a fixed user lock time validates lock; with LTIME = 0 lock follows the PLL status and its time depends on filter and target frequency. DPLLCTRLB.WUF (wake-up fast) opens the output gate at the end of start-up, before the frequency settles, saving several milliseconds. After first acquisition DPLLCTRLB.LBYPASS decides whether lock still gates the output. To change reference, disable it, change DPLLCTRLB.REFCLK, enable again. DPLLRATIO can be changed while running: LOCK clears and sets again when the output settles, and a falling lock edge sets INTFLAG.DPLLLCK (cleared by writing one). The PI filter tunes itself but DPLLCTRLB.FILTER can override it, and DPLLCTRLB.LPEN bypasses the TDC.

BOD33 watches the 3.3 V VDDANA supply and BOD12 the 1.2 V VDDCORE supply. Each compares against its LEVEL field and can reset the device or interrupt when the supply falls below it; PCLKSR.BOD33DET shows the BOD33 state. Threshold, action, hysteresis and enable are loaded from the Flash User Row at start-up and POR and can be overwritten. Continuous mode (MODE = 0, the default for both) watches all the time; BOD12 has no continuous mode in standby. Sampled mode (MODE = 1) powers the detector briefly on each tick of a sampling clock made from the OSCULP32K 1 kHz output by PSEL. Since that clock is asynchronous, writes to BOD33 or BOD12 are ignored while PCLKSR.B33SRDY or B12SRDY is zero. Clear CEN before changing the prescaler; to change PSEL in sampled mode wait for the SRDY bit, then write PSEL. HYST adds hysteresis in either mode.

VREG makes VDDCORE. It is on after any reset and can be turned off with VREG.ENABLE = 0. VREG.LEVEL sets the output and is loaded from factory calibration at reset. VREG.VDDMON monitors the core supply and applies a power-on reset if it falls below a critical level, well below the BOD12 threshold; code restarts only once the core voltage is back.

VREF is a bandgap generator, factory calibrated at typical voltage and temperature with VREF.CAL loaded at reset, plus a temperature sensor whose output voltage is linear in temperature over CMIN to CMAX. VREF.TSEN turns the sensor on and it can be routed to the ADC; VREF.BGOUTEN routes the bandgap to the ADC. VREF.CALIB sets the bandgap level and can be overwritten.

Interrupt sources, each on a rising edge of its PCLKSR bit: XOSCRDY, XOSC32KRDY, OSC32KRDY, OSC8MRDY, DFLLRDY, DFLLOOB, DFLLLOCKF, DFLLLOCKC, DFLLRCS, BOD33RDY, BOD33DET, B33SRDY, BOD12RDY, BOD12DET, B12SRDY; and for the FDPLL96M, LOCK (lock asserted), LOCKL (lock lost, a falling lock edge in normal operation) and LTTO (the DPLLCTRLB.LTIME time has passed since start). All share one request line to the NVIC, so software reads INTFLAG.

Check PCLKSR.DFLLRDY before writing any DFLL48M control register; writes while it is zero are ignored. To read a DFLL48M register, write DFLLSYNC.READREQ and read once DFLLRDY is set; reading without it starts a synchronization and halts the bus until done (no halt while the DFLL is off). The BOD prescaler counters are asynchronous too: a write to BOD33 or BOD12 clears B33SRDY or B12SRDY until complete, and meanwhile writing that register or reading the written one stalls the bus.

The watchdog resets the system if software does not clear it within its time-out period, catching runaway or stuck code; an early-warning interrupt can come before the time-out. Window mode adds a closed period in which a clear also resets, catching code that clears too often. Once enabled it runs in active and all sleep modes from its own CPU-independent clock and still acts if the main clocks fail. Time-outs run from 8 to 16,000 cycles in normal mode, 16 to 32,000 cycles in window mode. It has an always-on option.

CLK_WDT_APB is on by default. GCLK_WDT must be set up and enabled; it is meant to come from the ultra-low-power 32 kHz oscillator, whose limited accuracy makes the time-out vary between devices, which software must allow for. A more accurate source can be used at the cost of power. The WDT runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its interrupt can wake the device. In debug halt it stops, unless forced to keep running. INTFLAG is never write-protected by the PAC.

CTRL.WEN, CTRL.ALWAYSON, CTRL (all but ENABLE), CONFIG and EWCTRL are enable-protected: writes while CTRL.ENABLE is one are dropped, and writes made during disabling complete afterwards, so configure it while disabled. Normal mode needs CONFIG.PER; with early warning also EWCTRL.EWOFFSET and INTENSET.EW. Window mode needs CONFIG.PER, CONFIG.WINDOW and CTRL.WEN; with early warning also EWOFFSET and INTENSET.EW. At power-on, CTRL.ENABLE, CTRL.ALWAYSON, CTRL.WEN, CONFIG.WINDOW, CONFIG.PER and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET load from the NVM User Row. CTRL.ENABLE turns it on and off; it can be turned off only while ALWAYSON is zero.

CONFIG.PER chooses one of 12 time-out periods from 8 ms to 16 s. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR restarts the period and may be done at any time; writing any other value resets the system at once. By default a time-out resets and the early warning is off; INTENSET.EW turns it on and INTENCLR.EW off. EWCTRL.EWOFFSET gives the early warning's time as a number of GCLK_WDT cycles from the start of the period: with PER = 0x2 and EWOFFSET = 0x1 the warning comes at 16 cycles and the reset at 32. An offset beyond the period means the reset comes first and the warning never.

The period is a closed window (CONFIG.WINDOW, 8 ms to 16 s) in which a clear resets the system, followed by an open window (CONFIG.PER, 8 ms to 16 s) in which it may be cleared; the total is their sum. The early warning, if enabled, comes at the start of the open window, which suits a sleeping system that wakes, clears the watchdog and goes on or back to sleep.

Writing CTRL.ALWAYSON makes the WDT run whatever CTRL.ENABLE says; only a power-on reset clears it. CONFIG and EWCTRL become read-only, so PER, WINDOW and EWOFFSET are fixed, but CTRL.WEN can still switch window mode and the early warning can still be enabled or disabled.

The one interrupt source is the early warning, on one request line. CTRL and CLEAR are write-synchronized: STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done, INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal completion, and another synchronized access while busy stalls the bus, holding the CPU with interrupts pending.

The Real-Time Counter is a 32-bit counter behind a 10-bit prescaler that normally runs all the time to keep time, and can wake the device from sleep on an alarm or compare match, periodically, or on overflow. The usual and lowest-power clock is the 1.024 kHz output of OSC32K; the 32.768 kHz output gives better than 1 ms resolution, and other sources come through GCLK. It makes periodic events from the prescaler, alarm/compare interrupts and events at any count, and overflow interrupts and events, and can clear itself on a match for long, accurate periodic intervals. From 32.768 kHz the smallest tick is 30.5 µs and time-outs reach 36 hours; with a 1 s tick the longest time-out is over 136 years. Modes: 32-bit counter with one 32-bit compare, 16-bit counter with two 16-bit compares, or clock/calendar (seconds, minutes, hours in 12 or 24-hour form, day, month, year, leap-year correction), with digital frequency correction.

The RTC runs in every sleep mode and its interrupts can wake the device; its events act without waking it. Only POR or CTRL.SWRST resets it. CLK_RTC_APB is gated in the PM. GCLK_RTC must be set up and enabled; it is asynchronous to the bus clock. The RTC must never use generic clock generator 0. A 32.768 kHz crystal can go on XIN32 and XOUT32 with load capacitors. In debug halt it stops unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. INTFLAG, READREQ, STATUS and DBGCTRL are never write-protected by the PAC.

CTRL.MODE, CTRL.PRESCALER, CTRL.MATCHCLR, CTRL.CLKREP and EVCTRL are enable-protected: written only while CTRL.ENABLE is zero. Before enabling, choose the mode, the clock representation and the prescaler. In clock/calendar mode the prescaler must give the counter 1 Hz. CTRL.ENABLE turns it on and off; disable it before CTRL.SWRST, which resets every register but DBGCTRL and leaves it disabled.

Mode 0 (CTRL.MODE = 0): a 32-bit counter counting each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT up to 0xFFFFFFFF, wrapping to zero and setting INTFLAG.OVF; COUNT is read and written as 32 bits and compared with COMP0; a match sets INTFLAG.CMP0 on the next counter clock edge. With CTRL.MATCHCLR = 1 the counter clears on the cycle after a match, for periodic interrupts or events longer than the prescaler events, and CMP0 and OVF set together. Mode 1 (CTRL.MODE = 1): a 16-bit counter that counts to PER, wraps to zero and sets OVF, compared with COMP0 and COMP1. Mode 2 (CTRL.MODE = 2): clock/calendar, counting a 1 Hz clock in CLOCK as seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24-hour set by CTRL.CLKREP, changeable only while disabled), day of month from 1, month from 1, and year as an offset from a reference software defines. Every year divisible by 4 is taken as a leap year, so the reference must be a leap year such as 2000. It counts to 23:59:59 December 31 of year 63, then wraps to 00:00:00 January 1 of year 0 and sets OVF.

In clock/calendar mode CLOCK is compared with ALARM0; a match sets INTFLAG.ALARM0 on the next counter clock edge, so with a 1 Hz counter the flag comes 1 s after the match. MASK0.SEL chooses which time and date fields take part. With MATCHCLR = 1 the counter clears on the cycle after an alarm match, and ALARM0 and OVF set together.

Any of prescaler bits 2 to 9 can make an event on its rising edge when EVCTRL.PEREOn is set: PEREO0 every 8 GCLK_RTC cycles, PEREO1 every 16, and so on. They do not depend on the counter's prescaler setting, except that CTRL.PRESCALER = 0 gives no periodic events.

Needs CTRL.PRESCALER above 1. Once every 1024 GCLK_RTC cycles the prescaler can gain or skip one count; FREQCORR.VALUE says how many of 976 such periods get the adjustment, giving steps of about 1 ppm (resolution 1.0006 ppm). FREQCORR.SIGN gives the direction: positive speeds up, negative slows down. The correction also stretches or shortens the gap between periodic events at the end of a correction cycle.

Interrupts: overflow (OVF), compare n (CMPn), alarm n (ALARMn) and synchronization ready (SYNCRDY), on one request line, so software reads INTFLAG. Output events, each enabled by its EVCTRL bit: OVF, PERn, CMPn, ALARMn. The RTC runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs; on wake-up an interrupt follows if the NVIC is set for it, otherwise the CPU carries on after the sleep instruction. Periodic events can wake the CPU through an event system channel with its interrupt enabled.

Any RTC interrupt enabled in INTENSET can wake the device from shutdown if the RTC clock runs there. Afterwards every RTC register keeps its value except INTENCLR/SET (reset, all interrupts off), READREQ, INTFLAG and DBGCTRL; STATUS shows what happened during shutdown. The CPU starts from the reset address, and software must set up the NVIC and re-enable the RTC interrupts.

CTRL.SWRST and CTRL.ENABLE, and the registers COUNT, CLOCK, PER, COMPn, ALARMn, FREQCORR and MASKn, are synchronized on write; COUNT and CLOCK also on read. STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done; INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal it. Another synchronized access while busy stalls the bus, holding the CPU with interrupts pending.

The DMA controller moves data between memories and peripherals without the CPU and also holds a CRC engine. It has 6 channels, each with its own trigger (software, an event, or a dedicated peripheral request), automatic descriptor fetch and suspend/resume. An arbiter grants one channel at a time; the fetch engine loads that channel's transfer descriptor from SRAM, and a higher-priority channel can interrupt it, in which case the descriptor is written back to SRAM first. Interrupts and events can follow a transfer. Four bus interfaces: an AHB master for data, an APB slave for its registers, an AHB master for descriptor fetch and an AHB master for write-back. Transfers: peripheral to peripheral, peripheral to memory, memory to peripheral, memory to memory; single descriptors or linked lists for multi-buffer or circular buffers; 4 priority levels per channel, fixed or round-robin within a level; 1 to 256 kB in one block; static or incrementing addresses with configurable step; interrupts on block complete, error and suspend; event inputs and outputs on the 4 lowest channels; a write-back area per channel for error recovery; CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3).

The DMAC runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its interrupts can wake the device; in standby it is disabled internally but keeps its configuration. It needs CLK_DMAC_AHB, and CLK_DMAC_APB for its registers; the APB clock is synchronous to the AHB clock but can be divided and can run with the AHB clock off. Any reset sets all registers to their reset values. In debug halt it stops unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. INTPEND, CHID and CHINTFLAG are never write-protected by the PAC. No register synchronization is needed.

A beat is one bus access of BTCTRL.BEATSIZE. A burst is n beats, with n = 1 on this device, and cannot be interrupted. A block is what one descriptor moves, 1 to 64k beats, and can be interrupted between bursts. A transaction is all the blocks of a linked descriptor list. A transfer starts on a channel trigger; the channel asks the arbiter, and the granted channel runs as its descriptor says. An output event can follow each beat, and interrupts and an output event each block. When the transaction ends the channel is suspended or disabled as set.

BASEADDR and WRBADDR can be written only with the DMAC disabled (CTRL.DMAENABLE = 0); CTRL.SWRST only with both DMA and CRC disabled; CHCTRLB (except CMD and LVL) and CHCTRLA.SWRST only with the channel disabled; CRCCTRL and CRCCHKSUM only with the CRC disabled. Before enabling the DMAC write the descriptor section address to BASEADDR, the write-back section address to WRBADDR and enable the priority levels in CTRL.LVLENx. Before enabling a channel write its number to CHID, choose CHCTRLB.TRIGACT and TRIGSRC, and set up its first descriptor: BTCTRL.BEATSIZE, BTCTRL.VALID, BTCNT, SRCADDR and DSTADDR. For the CRC choose CRCCTRL.CRCSRC and CRCPOLY, and CRCBEATSIZE when the source is the I/O interface. CTRL.DMAENABLE, CHCTRLA.ENABLE (after CHID) and CTRL.CRCENABLE turn the parts on and off. CTRL.SWRST (with DMAC and CRC disabled) resets all but DBGCTRL; CHCTRLA.SWRST resets a disabled channel.

A channel's first descriptor must be valid before it is enabled and triggered. All descriptors live in SRAM. The first descriptors of all channels sit in one block at BASEADDR in channel order; the descriptors of ongoing blocks are kept in a write-back block at WRBADDR, also in channel order. Each section is 128 bits per channel up to the highest enabled channel, so using the lowest channels saves memory. The two sections can be separate, so a transaction repeats without rewriting its first descriptor, or the same (BASEADDR = WRBADDR), which uses less SRAM and shortens the delay from descriptor fetch to first burst. A descriptor holds BTCTRL, BTCNT, SRCADDR, DSTADDR and DESCADDR, the next descriptor's address.

An enabled, unsuspended channel that gets a trigger joins the pending queue and sets PENDCH.PENDCHx; when granted, PENDCHx clears and BUSYCH.BUSYCHx sets. After its burst the channel rejoins the queue (BUSYCHx stays set) or waits for a trigger, is suspended or disabled (BUSYCHx clears). A suspended pending channel leaves the queue but keeps PENDCHx and rejoins on resume; a disabled one leaves and clears PENDCHx. ACTIVE.LVLEXx shows a level pending or transferring. CHCTRLB.LVL sets a channel's level; with all levels enabled (CTRL.LVLENx) a lower level number wins. Within a level, PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx = 0 gives static priority (lower channel number first, which can starve high channels) and 1 gives round-robin, the last granted channel going lowest; its number is kept in PRICTRL0.LVLPRIx.

Once granted, the channel's descriptor is fetched from the descriptor section for a new block or the write-back section for an ongoing one, and data move from the current source to the current destination. Arbitration runs after each burst; BTCNT drops by the beats moved, and if another channel wins, the count goes to write-back memory ahead of fetching the new descriptor. At the end of a block (BTCNT = 0) VALID is cleared and the descriptor written back, with the transfer complete and suspend interrupts and the block event if set. If DESCADDR is 0x00000000 the transaction is over and the channel is suspended or disabled per BTCTRL.BLOCKACT; otherwise the next descriptor is fetched and copied to write-back memory ahead of the next arbitration.

A transfer starts only on a request from software, a peripheral or an event, chosen per channel in CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC. CHCTRLB.TRIGACT sets what a trigger starts: by default one block (a single-descriptor channel disables itself when the block is done; a linked list disables after its last descriptor or waits for the next trigger), or alternatively one beat or a whole transaction. A trigger during a transfer is held pending (CHSTATUS.PEND); only one can be held and further ones are lost. CHSTATUS.BUSY is set from start to completion of the action; PENDCH and BUSYCH show all channels.

Source and destination can each be static or incrementing. BTCTRL.SRCINC enables source increment; with BTCTRL.STEPSEL = 1 the step is BTCTRL.STEPSIZE, otherwise one beat. BTCTRL.DSTINC enables destination increment; with STEPSEL = 0 the step is STEPSIZE, otherwise one beat. With increment on, SRCADDR or DSTADDR must hold the address of the last beat of the block, not the first. Example: channel 0 stepping its source one beat and channel 1 two beats (STEPSEL = 1, STEPSIZE = 0x1), each writing to a fixed peripheral address.

A bus error from an AHB slave disables the active channel and sets CHINTFLAG.TERR (interrupt if enabled); BTCNT is not decremented and is written back before the channel stops. Fetching an invalid descriptor (VALID = 0), or resuming into a next address of 0x00000000, suspends the channel and sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and CHSTATUS.FERR.

A transaction of several blocks follows DESCADDR from each descriptor to the next until one with DESCADDR = 0x00000000. To append, build the new descriptor with DESCADDR = 0 and point the current last one at it. To change a descriptor in a live list: enable the suspend interrupt before enabling the channel; build the new descriptor (DESCADDR, DSTADDR, SRCADDR, BTCTRL with VALID and optionally suspend block action); clear VALID on the descriptor to change; read DESCADDR from write-back memory. If the DMA has not fetched it yet, update its DESCADDR, optionally clear the suspend action, set VALID and optionally resume. If the DMA is running it, suspend the channel and wait for the interrupt, update the write-back next address, clear the interrupt sources and resume, then update the list's DESCADDR, optionally clear the suspend action and set VALID. To insert C between A and B: impossible while B runs; if A has not started, clear A's VALID, point A at C and C at B, set A's VALID; if A is running, suspend the channel first, do the same, then resume.

Software suspends a channel with the suspend command in CHCTRLB.CMD, taking effect after the current burst and clearing itself; or BTCTRL.BLOCKACT can suspend after a block. A suspended channel stays enabled and takes triggers but leaves arbitration. Fetching an invalid descriptor also suspends it (CHSTATUS.FERR). Only an enabled channel can be suspended; disabling it clears a pending suspend. Suspension sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP. The resume command continues from where it stopped; given before a suspend, it makes the next suspend be skipped.

Only channels with event inputs (the 4 lowest) have these; CHCTRLB.EVACT picks the action and CHCTRLB.EVIE enables it, with the event system set up first; only resynchronized events are supported. Normal transfer (TRIGSRC = 0): the event triggers a beat or burst, is acknowledged at once and sets CHSTATUS.PEND; an event while pending is lost. Periodic transfer: the event gates a peripheral trigger chosen in TRIGSRC, for timed protocols or periodic peripheral-to-peripheral transfers; the peripheral request is registered only once an event comes and the previous action is done, and PEND sets when both are active. Conditional transfer: each peripheral trigger is registered when the event arrives, setting PEND and acknowledging the event; suited to one peripheral giving the event and another the DMA request. Conditional block: an event must arrive before a block starts and is acknowledged when the block completes. Channel suspend: acknowledged when the current AHB access ends. Channel resume: acknowledged at once and clears CHINTFLAG.SUSP. Skip next block suspend: resumes a suspended channel, or is held until the next block-suspend point, which is then skipped. In each conditional and periodic mode a software trigger also starts a transfer.

Channels with event outputs give a pulse one AHB clock wide after each beat, burst or block, as chosen in BTCTRL.EVOSEL and enabled by CHCTRLB.EVOE; for an event at the end of a transaction, select the block event in the last descriptor only. Disabling a channel aborts its transfers cleanly; disabling the DMAC aborts all: the active channel stops after its current beat and write-back, the others on the next clock. CHCTRLA.ENABLE and CTRL.DMAENABLE read zero once disabled.

A CRC-n detects any single error burst of up to n bits and the fraction 1 − 2^−n of longer bursts. Polynomials: CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT), the default, 0x1021, powers of x 16, 12, 5, 0; CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3), 0x04C11DB7, powers of x 32, 26, 23, 22, 16, 12, 11, 10, 8, 7, 5, 4, 2, 1, 0. The input is a DMA channel or the APB interface; the result is in CRCCHKSUM, bit-reversed and complemented for CRC-32. It works byte by byte. With a DMA channel as source it uses that channel's beat size and runs continuously on the data passing through, readable when the transaction completes or aborts; SRAM, Flash or I/O data can be checked by sending them through a DMA channel to CRCDATAIN. With the I/O interface set CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE (8, 16 or 32 bits) and write data to CRCDATAIN; a 32-bit write takes 4 cycles, and CRCSTATUS.CRCBUSY must be clear before the next write.

Per-channel interrupts: transfer complete (TCMPL, block done), transfer error (TERR, bus error or invalid descriptor) and suspend (SUSP), in CHINTFLAG with CHINTENSET and CHINTENCLR, all ORed into one NVIC request. INTSTATUS shows which channels have pending interrupts; INTPEND gives the lowest such channel and its flags. Output event CH after a block or a beat (CHCTRLB.EVOE with BTCTRL.EVOSEL). Input event actions: TRIG (normal or periodic transfer), CTRIG (conditional transfer), CBLOCK (conditional block), SUSPEND, RESUME and SSKIP (skip next block suspend), enabled by CHCTRLB.EVIE; with several events connected, every enabled action is taken for any of them.

The External Interrupt Controller turns 8 external pins (EXTINT[7:0]) into interrupt lines, plus one non-maskable pin (NMI) wired to the CPU's NMI request. Each line has its own interrupt flag and mask, senses rising, falling or both edges or high or low level, has a spike filter, can work asynchronously to wake the device from sleep modes with all clocks stopped, can make an event, and has a configurable wake-up.

Every interrupt works in every sleep mode, though the EIC can mask some automatically to prevent wake-up; events act without waking. CLK_EIC_APB is gated in the PM; GCLK_EIC, asynchronous to it, clocks the filters and edge detection. There are two request lines: EXTINT, which needs the NVIC set up, and NMI, which does not. Events are pulses. In debug halt it keeps running. INTFLAG and NMIFLAG are never write-protected by the PAC. Setup order: enable CLK_EIC_APB; enable GCLK_EIC if edge detection or filtering is used; write EVCTRL, WAKEUP and CONFIGy; enable the EIC (CTRL.ENABLE). When NMI is used, enable GCLK_EIC after writing NMICTRL. CTRL.SWRST resets every register and disables the EIC. Only CTRL.SWRST and CTRL.ENABLE are write-synchronized (STATUS.SYNCBUSY); no register needs synchronization.

CONFIGy.SENSEx sets each pin's sense (edge or level); INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] sets when the condition is met, with SENSEx non-zero. After clearing, an edge flag sets again only on a new edge, a level flag at once if the level persists. CONFIGy.FILTENx turns on a majority-vote filter that samples the pin three times on GCLK_EIC and outputs the value held by at least two samples. Level detection, or detection without the filter, is asynchronous and needs no GCLK_EIC; with filtering or edge detection the EIC requests GCLK_EIC itself, which must be enabled in GCLK.

operation.topic: EIC NMI, interrupts, events and wake-up
operation.text: NMI senses edges or level like the others but is set up in NMICTRL: NMISENSE selects the sense and enables detection (the EIC itself need not be enabled), NMIFILTEN the filter; after reset it detects nothing. A detection sets NMIFLAG.NMI, which always raises its interrupt request. EXTINT interrupts are enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR and share one request line; software reads INTFLAG (or NMIFLAG). EVCTRL.EXTINTEOx enables an event when pin x matches its CONFIGy setting. WAKEUP.WAKEUPEN[x] lets pin x wake the device from sleep when its condition matches; WAKEUPEN[x] = 1 with its interrupt disabled in INTENSET is not recommended.

The NVM Controller connects the Flash to the system: a 32-bit AHB interface for reads and writes, with every NVM section including calibration and configuration memory-mapped, and a 32-bit APB interface for commands and control. It has programmable read wait states, 16 regions that can each be locked, extra boot loader protection, a security bit for device protection, power-down of Flash blocks in sleep through the PM (waking either when sleep ends or at the first access) and a direct-mapped cache.

It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its interrupt can wake the device. The PM puts the NVM block in a low-power state on sleep as set by CTRLB.SLEEPPRM. It uses CLK_NVMCTRL_AHB and CLK_NVMCTRL_APB. At higher frequencies read wait states are needed; when the AHB frequency changes the wait states must be set to match. In debug it keeps running; the security bit can make the NVM inaccessible. INTFLAG and STATUS are never write-protected by the PAC. After power-up it runs a power-up sequence, halting AHB access, and then works with no configuration; it has no enable or reset.

The NVM is made of rows of four pages: erase works on a row, writes on a page, so four writes fill a row. A calibration and auxiliary space at NVM base + 0x00800000 holds factory calibration and system configuration and reads like the main array. The lowest rows of the main array can be a boot loader section set by the BOOTPROT fuses, protected by BOOTPROT[2:0] and its region lock bits; the top rows can be set aside for EEPROM emulation, which can be written whatever the region locks say.

The NVM is split into 16 equal regions, each with a lock bit against write and erase; all are unlocked when shipped. The Lock Region and Unlock Region commands act on the region holding the address in ADDR (written by software or left by a write) until the next reset; LOCK shows the state. The default lock state is changed by writing the user configuration in the auxiliary space with the Write Auxiliary Page command, effective after the next reset.

Reads and automatic page writes address the main array directly over AHB; manual page writes, erases and other operations are commands written to CTRLA.CMD together with the CTRLA.CMDEX key. INTFLAG.READY is low until a command completes and commands written meanwhile are ignored. CTRLB sets power reduction, read wait states (CTRLB.RWS) and write mode. Read data come after the RWS wait states. A row must be erased before programming; the whole array is erased by the debugger Chip Erase, single rows by Erase Row (all bits to one; in a locked region it is refused and STATUS.LOCKE sets). Data go first into a page-sized buffer, by 16 or 32-bit writes; an 8-bit write causes a system exception. Each AHB write stores its address in ADDR, and STATUS.LOAD shows the buffer is loaded. With MANW = 1, fill the buffer then issue Write Page with CMDEX. With MANW = 0 (the default) writing the last word of a page starts the write automatically; the row must be erased before that last write, and a partly filled page needs a manual write. During programming READY is low and AHB access stalls. The buffer resets to all ones after a page write; Page Buffer Clear empties a partly written buffer. Set and Clear Power Reduction Mode commands move the NVM in and out of power reduction (STATUS.PRM).

The user configuration is in the auxiliary space. The boot loader sits at offset zero of the main array and its section is write-protected. The EEPROM fuses reserve the top rows for EEPROM emulation, writable whatever the region locks.

The security bit locks the whole chip against external access. It is set by the Set Security Bit (SSB) command, after which STATUS.PROGE can be checked, and only a debugger Chip Erase clears it. The cache, a direct-mapped 8 lines of 64 bits (64 bytes), lowers power and speeds up execution when wait states are needed; CTRLB.CACHEDIS = 0 enables it and CTRLB.READMODE picks one of three modes. The INVALL command invalidates all lines, and commands that change NVM content invalidate lines automatically.

The PORT controls the I/O pins, grouped in sets of up to 32. Each pin is either general-purpose I/O, input or output with configurable drive and pull, or handed to a peripheral. Direction and output value can be set, cleared or toggled for any pins atomically with one 8, 16 or 32-bit write, without touching the others. The PORT sits on the bus matrix through an AHB/APB bridge, and its direction, output and input registers are also on the single-cycle CPU local bus (IOBUS). Each pin has its own input/output choice, software peripheral multiplexing, a pin configuration register, push-pull output with pull and drive strength settings, internal pull-up or pull-down, input sampling options, and an input buffer that can be turned off to save power.

Pins are named Pxy: x the group letter from A, y the bit number 00 to 31 (e.g. PA24). Some may not exist on a given device. A pin can have several peripheral functions; the selected peripheral controls the pad output and reads its state. During reset every pin is an input with input buffer, output buffer and pull disabled. If the PORT is shut down the pad latches keep output value and pull, but the configuration registers and input synchronizers lose their contents and must be set up again. It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs. CLK_PORT_APB is gated in the PM. The CPU main clock serves the IOBUS and the input synchronizers; the APB clock, a division of it, serves register access through the bridge. IOBUS accesses win over APB, which gets wait states when they clash. In debug it keeps running. Choosing an analog function on a pin turns off its digital features; analog blocks connect to pads directly.

The IOBUS is a single-cycle CPU-to-PORT interface with no wait states, for byte, half-word and word accesses at address 0x60000000, with the same register map. Through it DIRn and OUTn allow read, write, set, clear and toggle, and INn read. Because it cannot wait for input resynchronization, CTRLn must enable continuous sampling on every pin read over the IOBUS, or stale data may be read.

Writing one to a DIR bit makes the pin an output, zero an input; OUT sets the output level. PINCFG holds further settings. IN reads the pin through a synchronizer on the PORT clock, clocked only on a read by default to save power; it reads whether the pin is input or output unless PINCFG.INEN is zero. Setting PINCFG.PMUXEN and writing the selection to PMUX hands the pin to a peripheral line instead. After reset all standard pins are on the PORT with outputs tri-stated and inputs disabled, even with no clocks; special pins such as the debugger's may differ. Pin y's register set is at PORT + (y / 32) × 0x80 and bit (y % 32) indexes it. DIRSET, DIRCLR, OUTSET, OUTCLR and OUTTGL change single bits without disturbing others. An input reads in IN once PINCFG.INEN is set. An on-demand synchronizer delays a read by two CLK_PORT cycles; setting CTRL.SAMPLINGn, n = (y % 32) / 8, keeps a group of eight synchronizers always running, at more power. PINCFGy is at byte offset PINCFG0 + (y % 32). The function is chosen in PMUXn at byte offset PMUX0 + (y % 32) / 2, bits 3:0 (PMUXE) for even y and bits 7:4 (PMUXO) for odd y; the peripheral must also be set up and enabled.

PINCFG sets totem-pole, open-drain or pull configurations; since pull is set there, no intermediate states occur while direction and value change. With pull enabled, OUT chooses pull-up (1) or pull-down (0). A totem-pole output drives OUT's level with no current limit other than the pin's own; an input with no pull floats. Enabling the output driver turns pull off.

The Event System passes signals (events) straight from peripherals that make them (generators) to peripherals that act on them (users), with low latency and without the CPU, the bus or RAM. It has 6 channels, each able to connect any generator through an asynchronous, synchronous or resynchronized path; 18 generators and 44 users; a configurable edge detector; SleepWalking and an interrupt for low-power operation; software events; and each user picks the channel it listens to.

The event system can wake the CPU from every sleep mode even with its channel clock and bus clock off. When a generator raises an event while the system clock is stopped, a synchronous or resynchronized channel restarts its generic clock GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNELx just long enough to handle the event, leaving the device asleep (SleepWalking); an asynchronous path needs no clock. A software reset returns all registers to reset values and cancels events in progress. CLK_EVSYS_APB is gated in the PM; each channel's generic clock must be set up and enabled before use. In debug halt it keeps running. INTFLAG is never write-protected by the PAC. The module is always enabled; CTRL.SWRST resets it.

Set up the generator to make events and the user to accept them, then: first the user, with one 16-bit write to USER giving the channel in USER.CHANNEL and the user in USER.USER; then the channel, with one 32-bit write to CHANNEL giving CHANNEL.CHANNEL, the path in CHANNEL.PATH, the edge detection in CHANNEL.EDGSEL and the generator in CHANNEL.EVGEN. Each user has its own multiplexer that takes every channel and selects one; users are always set up ahead of channels. To read back a user, do an 8-bit write to USER.USER and read USER as 16 bits; to read a channel, an 8-bit write to CHANNEL.CHANNEL, then read CHANNEL. By default no channel has a generator (EVGEN = 0x00).

Asynchronous: the event goes from generator to user with no event-system logic, even with the channel clock off; no interrupts, no channel status, no edge detection (the user must handle edges); the lowest latency when generator and user share a generic clock. Synchronous: for a generator on the same generic clock as the channel; otherwise a change may be missed and the event lost. Resynchronized: for a generator on a different clock; the channel resynchronizes the event. Both synchronous and resynchronized paths can raise interrupts and update CHSTATUS. With CTRL.GCLKREQ = 0 they request their generic clock only when an event passes (SleepWalking); with GCLKREQ = 1 the clock stays on.

operation.topic: EVSYS edge detection, status and software events
operation.text: Synchronous and resynchronized paths need edge detection, set in CHANNEL.EDGSEL: rising, falling or both. A generator that gives pulses cannot use both edges; use rising or falling according to its idle level. CHSTATUS.CHBUSYx is one while some user of channel x has yet to handle its event; CHSTATUS.USRRDYx is one when all its users are ready. Writing CHANNEL.SWEVT together with CHANNEL.CHANNEL makes a software event on that channel, behaving like any generator; it needs a synchronous or resynchronized path (CHANNEL.PATH = 0x0 or 0x1), rising-edge detection (CHANNEL.EDGSEL = 0x1) and CTRL.GCLKREQ = 0x1.

Per channel, an overrun flag (INTFLAG.OVRx) sets when a user on channel x is not ready for a new event or an event arrives before the last was handled by all users, and an event-detected flag (INTFLAG.EVDx) sets when the channel's generator event is detected; neither works on the asynchronous path. All share one request line. The event system can wake the device from any sleep mode with an interrupt.

Each SERCOM is one serial engine that is set up as an I2C (SMBus compatible), SPI or USART interface; once enabled in a mode, all its resources serve that mode. It has a transmitter with a single buffer, a receiver with a two-level buffer, a baud-rate generator and address match/mask logic. It can run from its generic clock or an external clock, which lets it work in every sleep mode, and it can be served by DMA. Its signals leave through four pads, PAD[3:0], each routed to pins through the PORT multiplexer; which mode signal sits on which pad is chosen in the mode's own settings.

The bus clock CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on by default and gated in the PM. Two generic clocks serve it: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE, needed when the SERCOM is a master, and GCLK_SERCOMx_SLOW, needed only for some functions; both are set up and enabled in the GCLK before use and are asynchronous to the bus clock, so writes to some registers need synchronization. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC; the SERCOM has no events. In debug halt it keeps running unless set to halt. All writable registers can be write-protected by the PAC except INTFLAG, ADDR and DATA; protection is lifted while the CPU is halted in debug. The SERCOM works in any sleep mode in which its serial clock (external, or from its own baud-rate generator) runs, and its interrupts can wake the device.

On the transmit side sit one write buffer and a shift register; on the receive side a shift register feeding a two-level buffer. Clocking comes from the baud-rate generator, which runs on GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE or an external clock and gives /1, /2 and /16 outputs: asynchronous transmit uses /16 and asynchronous receive /1, synchronous operation uses /2, chosen automatically by the mode. Address matching serves SPI and I2C.
CTRLA.MODE picks the mode. CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables the SERCOM and 0 disables it. CTRLA.SWRST = 1 returns every register except DBGCTRL to its reset value and disables the SERCOM.

The output frequency fBAUD is set by the BAUD register and the reference fREF, which is the serial engine clock, internal or external. Asynchronous arithmetic mode uses a 16-bit BAUD value (0 to 65,535). Asynchronous fractional mode uses a 13-bit BAUD value, which must be 1 or more, plus a 3-bit fractional part FP; it is the mode used for auto-baud detection. Synchronous mode uses an 8-bit BAUD value (0 to 255). S, the samples per bit, is 16, 8 or 3.

The address logic compares 7 or 8 bits, by mode, in one of three ways. Address with mask: ADDR.ADDR is compared with the received address, ignoring every bit set in ADDR.ADDRMASK; a mask of all zeros matches one address and all ones accepts every address. Two unique addresses: a match on either ADDR or ADDRMASK. Address range: any address from ADDR.ADDRMASK (lower limit) to ADDR.ADDR (upper limit), both included.

Interrupt sources depend on the mode. Each has a flag in INTFLAG, set by its condition, enabled by writing one to its INTENSET bit and disabled through INTENCLR; a request holds until its flag is cleared, the source is disabled, or the SERCOM is put through a reset. All sources share one request line, so INTFLAG is read to find the cause. Registers that cross from CLK_SERCOMx_APB to GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE may need synchronization on write, on read, on both or not at all. STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once when such an access starts and clears when it finishes; a Synchronization Ready interrupt can signal the end. Another synchronized access while SYNCBUSY is one stalls the bus until it is done; it completes, but the CPU waits and interrupts stay pending.

USART is a SERCOM mode: full duplex, asynchronous with clock recovery or synchronous, internal or external clock in either, frames of 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 data bits with 1 or 2 stop bits, odd or even parity generated and checked, LSB or MSB first. It detects buffer overflow and frame errors, filters noise with false start-bit detection and a digital low-pass filter, detects collisions, works in all sleep modes, runs up to half the system clock with an internal clock and up to the system clock with an external one, and offers RTS/CTS flow control, IrDA modulation up to 115.2 kbps, LIN slave support, auto-baud and break detection, start-of-frame detection and DMA. The transmitter's write buffer allows frames back to back; the receiver has a two-level buffer.

It keeps running in any sleep mode in which its clock source runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is gated in the PM; GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up and enabled in the GCLK before use and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register writes need synchronization. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt to the NVIC; there are no events. It keeps running in debug halt unless DBGCTRL halts it. All writable registers can be PAC protected except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; protection is lifted during debug halt and never applies to an external debugger.

Three lines: RxD receives, TxD transmits, XCK carries the clock in synchronous operation. A frame is one start bit (always low), 5 to 9 data bits sent MSB or LSB first, an optional even or odd parity bit after the data, and 1 or 2 stop bits (always high). A frame may follow straight on from the last, or the line idles high.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN and TXEN) and BAUD can be written only while the USART is disabled; writes while it is enabled or being enabled are dropped, and writes while it is being disabled take effect once disabled.
